_nota: Initial answers to the five questions. Starting hypotheses: each row is validated with a local advisor. E4 and E5 have no validated local data. Same content and same keys as strategies.es.json.

labels.risks: What to check with your technician

E0.name: Maize → bare soil → maize
E0.summary: What you do today: rain-fed maize, with the plot bare in the dry season.
E0.why: It is your current rotation. We measure it with the same yardstick as the other five.

evidence.detail: Your plot has no green plants from November to March.
The first rains of the season arrive heavy, in your area.
Days of strong heat when the maize flowers, in your area.

benefits: No change in seed, labor or market.
You already know it and how your plot responds.
missing: How much soil your plot loses each season.
Whether maize yield has dropped over the years.
risks: Signs of erosion after the first rains.
Pests that build up with several years of maize in a row.

E1.name: Maize + velvet bean → mulch → maize
E1.summary: A legume cover crop, such as velvet bean or jack bean, grows as a relay and leaves mulch in the dry season.
E1.why: Your plot is bare in the dry season and gets heavy rain at the start of the season.

evidence.detail: No green plants from November to March on your plot.
Months without green plants around your plot, since 2000.
Terrain slope, which speeds up running water.
Heavy rain at the start of the season, in your area.

benefits: Less erosion: the mulch shields the soil from heavy rain.
You might need less nitrogen fertilizer.
More organic matter over the years.
missing: How much nitrogen it adds on your plot.
Whether it competes with maize for water in dry years.
risks: Planting date of the relay crop.
Velvet bean is not fodder without treatment.
Dry mulch can raise the risk of fire.

E2.name: Maize → regional bean → maize
E2.summary: One year of regional bean between two years of maize.
E2.why: Several years of maize in a row build up pests. Beans are part of the milpa and sell locally.

evidence.detail: Water the bean needs at each stage, against the rain of past years.
Rain in past seasons, in your area.
Bean price and planted area in the region.

benefits: One more sale in the cycle.
Leaves nitrogen for the next maize.
Spreads the risk across two crops.
missing: The local price when you harvest.
Yield of the local variety on your soil.

E3.name: Maize → sorghum → maize
E3.summary: One year of sorghum between two years of maize.
E3.why: In dry years, maize runs short of water or gets hit by heat right at flowering.

evidence.detail: How often rain fails at flowering, in your area.
Days of heat that harms the crop, on your plot.
How it would do in a very dry season.

benefits: Lower risk of losing the harvest in a dry year.
missing: Price and buyer for sorghum in your area.
risks: Effect of the stubble on the next maize.

E4.name: Maize → chickpea → maize
E4.summary: One year of chickpea between two years of maize.
E4.why: It is a legume other than beans. We include it to compare more rotation crops.

evidence.detail: Water chickpea needs at each stage. Validated values for your area are missing.
Rain in past seasons, in your area.
Heat in past seasons, in your area.

benefits: It might leave nitrogen for the next maize, being a legume.
It might spread the risk across two crops.
missing: Chickpea is uncommon in your area. There is no validated local data.
Its yield and its price: that is why we do not compare its income.
How much water it needs and how much heat it stands on your plot.
risks: Whether chickpea grows in the heat of your area.
Where to get seed and who buys it.

E5.name: Maize → wheat → maize
E5.summary: One year of wheat between two years of maize.
E5.why: It is a cereal other than sorghum. We include it to compare more rotation crops.

evidence.detail: Water wheat needs at each stage. Validated values for your area are missing.
Rain in past seasons, in your area.
Heat in past seasons, in your area.

benefits: It might give one more sale in the cycle, if there is a buyer.
The stubble might leave cover on the soil.
missing: Wheat is uncommon in your area. There is no validated local data.
Its yield and its price: that is why we do not compare its income.
How much water it needs and how much heat it stands on your plot.
risks: Whether wheat grows in the heat of your area.
Whether machinery is needed to harvest it.
Where to get seed and who buys it.

E2.name: Maize → xpelón → maize
E2.summary: One year of xpelón, the Yucatecan bean, between two years of maize.
missing: The local price when you harvest.
Yield of xpelón on your soil.
Whether xpelón stands heat and drought better. It is a hypothesis with no source yet.
risks: Planting date and days to harvest for xpelón.

E2.name: Maize → ib → maize
E2.summary: One year of ib, the regional lima bean, between two years of maize.
missing: The local price when you harvest.
Yield of ib on your soil.
risks: Planting date and days to harvest for ib.

E2.name: Maize → black bean → maize
E2.summary: One year of black bean between two years of maize.
missing: The local price when you harvest.
Yield of black bean on your soil.
risks: Planting date and days to harvest for black bean.

reasons.noMachinery: Without a tractor or hired service, harvesting {crop} by hand is not viable on this area.
reasons.heatThinSoil: With extreme heat and thin soil, {crop} might not grow.

rules.notAccepted: If you don't want to plant a crop, its option is left out.
rules.noMarket: With nowhere to sell, beans, chickpea, sorghum and wheat are left out.
rules.noMachinery: Without a tractor or hired service, sorghum and wheat are left out.
rules.heatThinSoil: With extreme heat and thin soil, chickpea and wheat are marked hardly viable.
rules.nitrogen: Only legumes add nitrogen: beans and chickpea do; sorghum and wheat do not.

variantChosenBy.team: The kinilum team chose it for this illustrative case. On a real plot your technician chooses it.
